Ons belongs with singular het netwerk; moet leren is a final verb group. weten: present forms weet / weet / weten; past singular wist, plural wisten; perfect heb geweten. Necessity or obligation; a following infinitive has no te. In a perfect verb cluster: heb moeten werken. leren: present forms leer / leert / leren; past singular leerde, plural leerden; perfect heb geleerd. Learning a skill; leren kennen means become acquainted with.
career-office-048.compare: English usually keeps subject–verb–object inside the embedded clause; Dutch moves the finite verb/group toward its end.

mistake.wrong: Ik weten dat ik nog veel over ons netwerk moet leren.
mistake.right: Ik weet dat ik nog veel over ons netwerk moet leren.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form weet here. weten is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-048.meaning: I know that I still have a lot to learn about our network. During a learning review, acknowledge to your mentor that there is still a lot you need to learn about the team's network.

career-office-049.order: The finite verb Kan comes before subject ik. The finite modal comes before the subject. The requested action stays an infinitive without te. Whether this asks about ability, permission or willingness depends on the actual modal and context.
career-office-049.forms: Samen met jou identifies collaboration, not handing the task over entirely. Eerst places the joint attempt before independent work. kunnen: present forms kan / kan / kunnen; past singular kon, plural konden; perfect heb gekund. Kan/kunt with je are both standard; before subject je use kan/kun. A following action infinitive has no te. uitvoeren: present forms voer uit / voert uit / voeren uit; past singular voerde uit, plural voerden uit; perfect heb uitgevoerd. Separable: uitvoeren, voer uit, uit te voeren, uitgevoerd.
career-office-049.compare: English can/could/may are not interchangeable in every situation; preserve the intended ability or permission distinction.

mistake.wrong: Kunnen ik deze taak eerst samen met jou uitvoeren?
mistake.right: Kan ik deze taak eerst samen met jou uitvoeren?
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form Kan here. kunnen is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-049.meaning: Can I carry out this task with you first? You are about to perform an unfamiliar task. Ask your colleague informally whether you can do it together the first time.

parts.label: infinitive (te phrase)
parts.text: om de stappen later zelfstandig te herhalen.

career-office-050.order: The first constituent is Ik; maak is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. Om introduces an infinitive phrase with te. Its object can come before the infinitive; with a separable verb te stands between its particle and verb. This is not a second finite clause.
career-office-050.forms: The om te phrase expresses a learning purpose. Later distinguishes independent repetition from the current demonstration. maken: present forms maak / maakt / maken; past singular maakte, plural maakten; perfect heb gemaakt. Make/do; compare een fout maken and een reservekopie maken. herhalen: present forms herhaal / herhaalt / herhalen; past singular herhaalde, plural herhaalden; perfect heb herhaald. Repeat; inseparable her- means no ge- in herhaald.
career-office-050.compare: English often uses to plus a verb for purpose where Dutch uses om ... te.

mistake.wrong: Ik maken aantekeningen om de stappen later zelfstandig te herhalen.
mistake.right: Ik maak aantekeningen om de stappen later zelfstandig te herhalen.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form maak here. maken is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-050.meaning: I take notes so I can repeat the steps independently later. A colleague is demonstrating a task to you. Explain that you are taking notes so that you can repeat the steps on your own later.

career-office-051.order: The first constituent is Ik; werk is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. A normal declarative main clause has one first constituent and then its finite verb. The subject can be that first constituent. Other phrases can appear inside the verb bracket.
career-office-051.forms: Van thuis uit is standard Belgian wording for working from home. The sentence states frequency without naming the days. werken: present forms werk / werkt / werken; past singular werkte, plural werkten; perfect heb gewerkt. Werken aan introduces a task; op de servicedesk describes the workplace.
career-office-051.compare: English often uses a similar subject–verb order, but Dutch keeps the finite verb second when another complete phrase comes first.

mistake.wrong: Ik werken twee dagen per week van thuis uit.
mistake.right: Ik werk twee dagen per week van thuis uit.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form werk here. werken is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-051.meaning: I work from home two days a week. A colleague asks about your regular work arrangement. Explain that you work from home two days each week.

career-office-052.order: The first constituent is Op mijn thuiswerkdag; ben is the finite main verb and ik is its subject. The complete time, place or object phrase is one first constituent. The finite verb follows it, then the subject: second position means a constituent, not the second written word.
career-office-052.forms: The complete day phrase is first, so ben precedes ik. Dezelfde means the same rather than merely a similar group. zijn: present forms ben / is / zijn; past singular was, plural waren; perfect ben geweest. State or identity; zijn is irregular.
career-office-052.compare: English can keep subject before verb after an initial time phrase; Dutch uses inversion here.

mistake.wrong: Op mijn thuiswerkdag zijn ik via dezelfde chatgroep bereikbaar.
mistake.right: Op mijn thuiswerkdag ben ik via dezelfde chatgroep bereikbaar.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form ben here. zijn is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-052.meaning: On my work-from-home day, I am reachable through the same chat group. A teammate asks how to contact you while you work from home. Say that the same chat group can be used on that day.

parts.label: subordinate clause
parts.text: omdat de nieuwe medewerker begeleiding nodig heeft.

career-office-053.order: The first constituent is Ik; kom is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. The main clause retains its own finite-verb position. The conjunction introduces a separate clause whose subject and other material precede its finite verb or verb group. The conjunction's meaning must fit the situation.
career-office-053.forms: Omdat gives a reason, not a condition. Nodig heeft closes the subordinate clause; tomorrow's visit is an arrangement. komen: present forms kom / komt / komen; past singular kwam, plural kwamen; perfect ben gekomen. Arrival normally forms the perfect with zijn. hebben: present forms heb / heeft / hebben; past singular had, plural hadden; perfect heb gehad. Possession or auxiliary; hebben is irregular.
career-office-053.compare: English usually keeps subject–verb–object inside the embedded clause; Dutch moves the finite verb/group toward its end.

mistake.wrong: Ik komen morgen naar kantoor omdat de nieuwe medewerker begeleiding nodig heeft.
mistake.right: Ik kom morgen naar kantoor omdat de nieuwe medewerker begeleiding nodig heeft.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form kom here. komen is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-053.meaning: I am coming to the office tomorrow because the new employee needs guidance. Your colleague asks why you will be in the office tomorrow. Explain that the new employee needs guidance there.

career-office-054.order: The first constituent is Ik; ben is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. Geen negates an indefinite noun phrase or an uncountable amount. Niet negates a verb/state or another specific constituent. Nog niet means not yet; niet meer means no longer. The position depends on the intended scope.
career-office-054.forms: Niet negates reachability through that specific number. It does not say that every contact method is unavailable. zijn: present forms ben / is / zijn; past singular was, plural waren; perfect ben geweest. State or identity; zijn is irregular.
career-office-054.compare: English often uses not or no where Dutch distinguishes niet from geen.

mistake.wrong: Ik zijn thuis niet op het interne telefoonnummer bereikbaar.
mistake.right: Ik ben thuis niet op het interne telefoonnummer bereikbaar.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form ben here. zijn is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-054.meaning: I cannot be reached on the internal extension at home. A colleague tries to use your internal extension while you work remotely. Explain that this number does not reach you at home.

career-office-055.order: The finite verb Kunnen comes before subject we. The finite modal comes before the subject. The requested action stays an infinitive without te. Whether this asks about ability, permission or willingness depends on the actual modal and context.
career-office-055.forms: Kunnen expresses a proposed practical option. The question does not claim that a handover has already taken place. kunnen: present forms kan / kan / kunnen; past singular kon, plural konden; perfect heb gekund. Kan/kunt with je are both standard; before subject je use kan/kun. A following action infinitive has no te. doen: present forms doe / doet / doen; past singular deed, plural deden; perfect heb gedaan. Do; irregular deed and gedaan.
career-office-055.compare: English can/could/may are not interchangeable in every situation; preserve the intended ability or permission distinction.

mistake.wrong: Kan we de overdracht via een videogesprek doen?
mistake.right: Kunnen we de overdracht via een videogesprek doen?
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form Kunnen here. kan is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-055.meaning: Can we do the handover through a video call? You and a colleague will be in different locations at shift change. Ask whether the handover can take place through a video call.

career-office-056.order: The first constituent is Ik; heb is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. The finite auxiliary is in the main-clause verb position. Its object, pronouns and other phrases can stand before the participle that closes the bracket. Auxiliary choice depends on the actual verb and meaning.
career-office-056.forms: Afgestemd is the separable participle. Met identifies the person consulted; the statement concerns an agreed arrangement. hebben: present forms heb / heeft / hebben; past singular had, plural hadden; perfect heb gehad. Possession or auxiliary; hebben is irregular. afstemmen: present forms stem af / stemt af / stemmen af; past singular stemde af, plural stemden af; perfect heb afgestemd. Separable: coordinate afstemmen met a person, or op a requirement/each other.
career-office-056.compare: English past reporting may correspond to Dutch perfect; Dutch often puts the object before the final participle.

mistake.wrong: Ik hebben mijn thuiswerkdag met de teamleider afgestemd.
mistake.right: Ik heb mijn thuiswerkdag met de teamleider afgestemd.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form heb here. hebben is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-056.meaning: I have agreed my work-from-home day with the team leader. A colleague asks whether your remote-work arrangement has been coordinated. Say that you have agreed the day with the team leader.

career-office-057.order: The first constituent is Ik; ben is the finite main verb and Ik is its subject. A finite form of zijn describes the ongoing state. Aan het is followed by an infinitive, not an extra finite verb. For separable verbs more than one progressive placement can be natural.
career-office-057.forms: Aan het klaarmaken describes preparation in progress. It does not imply the workstation is already ready. zijn: present forms ben / is / zijn; past singular was, plural waren; perfect ben geweest. State or identity; zijn is irregular. klaarmaken: present forms maak klaar / maakt klaar / maken klaar; past singular maakte klaar, plural maakten klaar; perfect heb klaargemaakt. Separable: get ready/prepare; klaar te maken.
career-office-057.compare: English be plus an -ing form often corresponds to Dutch zijn aan het plus infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik zijn mijn thuiswerkplek aan het klaarmaken.
mistake.right: Ik ben mijn thuiswerkplek aan het klaarmaken.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form ben here. zijn is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-057.meaning: I am getting my home workstation ready. Before starting a remote shift, a colleague asks what you are doing now. Explain that you are currently preparing your home workstation.

career-office-058.order: The first question constituent is Welke taken; kunnen is the finite verb. A question word/phrase comes first, then the finite verb and subject. In a subject question the question phrase itself is the subject, so no extra subject is needed.
career-office-058.forms: Even goed means equally well, not briefly well. The question concerns practical suitability, not blanket permission. kunnen: present forms kan / kan / kunnen; past singular kon, plural konden; perfect heb gekund. Kan/kunt with je are both standard; before subject je use kan/kun. A following action infinitive has no te. uitvoeren: present forms voer uit / voert uit / voeren uit; past singular voerde uit, plural voerden uit; perfect heb uitgevoerd. Separable: uitvoeren, voer uit, uit te voeren, uitgevoerd.
career-office-058.compare: English often inserts do/does; Dutch normally puts the finite verb before the subject instead.

mistake.wrong: Welke taken kan we even goed op afstand uitvoeren?
mistake.right: Welke taken kunnen we even goed op afstand uitvoeren?
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form kunnen here. kan is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-058.meaning: Which tasks can we carry out just as well remotely? Your team is comparing remote and office work. Ask which tasks can be carried out equally well remotely.

career-office-059.order: The first constituent is Tijdens mijn vorige thuiswerkdag; had is the finite main verb and ik is its subject. The finite past form occupies the ordinary main-clause verb position. Its number agrees with the subject. The past event belongs to the context supplied, not automatically to every repeated or present situation.
career-office-059.forms: Had is singular past. Regelmatig means regularly; it does not mean continuously or on one specific channel. hebben: present forms heb / heeft / hebben; past singular had, plural hadden; perfect heb gehad. Possession or auxiliary; hebben is irregular.
career-office-059.compare: Dutch uses a single finite past verb here; English did is not added to the Dutch construction.

mistake.wrong: Tijdens mijn vorige thuiswerkdag hadden ik regelmatig contact met de servicedesk.
mistake.right: Tijdens mijn vorige thuiswerkdag had ik regelmatig contact met de servicedesk.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form had here. hadden is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-059.meaning: During my previous work-from-home day, I had regular contact with the service desk. Your manager asks about communication on your previous remote-working day. Report that you were in regular contact with the service desk.

career-office-060.order: The first constituent is Als ik van locatie verander,; werk is the finite main verb and ik is its subject. The complete subordinate clause counts as the first constituent of the main clause. The main finite verb follows it, then the main subject. Inside the subordinate clause its own verb/group comes toward the end.
career-office-060.forms: The whole als-clause is the first constituent; werk follows before ik. Bijwerken splits as werk ... bij in the main clause. bijwerken: present forms werk bij / werkt bij / werken bij; past singular werkte bij, plural werkten bij; perfect heb bijgewerkt. Separable: update; bij te werken. veranderen: present forms verander / verandert / veranderen; past singular veranderde, plural veranderden; perfect heb veranderd / ben veranderd. Hebben when changing an object; zijn when the subject itself changes state.
career-office-060.compare: English can keep the main subject before the verb after an initial when/if/because clause; Dutch uses main-clause inversion.

mistake.wrong: Als ik van locatie verander, bijwerken ik mijn bereikbaarheid in de agenda bij.
mistake.right: Als ik van locatie verander, werk ik mijn bereikbaarheid in de agenda bij.
mistake.why: The stated subject and tense require the finite form werk here. bijwerken is not the matching finite form for this sentence; an infinitive is not automatically a finite verb.

career-office-060.meaning: When I change location, I update my contact availability in the calendar. A teammate asks how they can find your current availability. Explain the routine you follow whenever you change work location.
